companyCaseStudy.title: How Zoom Scaled from ~10M to 300M Daily Meeting Participants: cutting join latency, autoscaling media, and surviving the COVID surge
companyCaseStudy.summary: Zoom went from ~10M to ~300M daily meeting participants in a few months in 2020, forcing a complete re-think of real-time media infrastructure. They separated signaling from media, built aggressive autoscaling for media servers, leaned into UDP/TURN optimization, and improved join latency from seconds to sub-2s for many users while keeping costs and outages under control.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
In early 2020 Zoom saw a surge from roughly 10 million daily meeting participants to ~300 million daily meeting participants in just a few months — a ~30x growth in usage that instantly turned any inefficiency into an outage. That growth stressed real-time media, NAT traversal, control-plane capacity, and ops processes.

## Problem: what broke when scale exploded
- Signaling (meeting control) endpoints became hotspots: account joins, breakout management, presence updates spiked.
- Media servers (SFU/MCU) hit CPU and network saturation, increasing join times and packet loss.
- NAT traversal (ICE/TURN) demand skyrocketed — TURN relays became bandwidth bottlenecks and expensive.
- Global distribution gaps caused uneven quality: some regions saw 3–5x worse packet loss and much longer join times.
- Manual capacity ops couldn't keep up — provisioning media hosts by hand created long lead times and outages.

Numbers to make this concrete:
- Daily meeting participants: ~10M -> ~300M (Jan–Apr 2020)
- Concurrent meetings: tens of thousands -> hundreds of thousands of concurrent meetings
- TURN traffic ballooned by multiple orders of magnitude (bandwidth costs soared)
- Initial median join time in stressed regions: ~6–8s; tail join times > 20s

## Challenge
Real-time video is unforgiving: join latency and packet loss directly impact user experience. Scaling a control plane is easier than scaling distributed media transport across millions of untrusted networks (NATs, firewalls, mobile carriers). Zoom had to: 1) reduce join latency, 2) avoid explosive costs from TURN bandwidth, 3) scale media servers elastically, and 4) improve reliability globally — all while demand moved orders of magnitude faster than usual capacity planning cycles.

## Solution — a set of engineering decisions
Zoom applied a combination of architectural separation, autoscaling, protocol and network optimizations, and operational automation.

### 1) Separation of concerns: signaling vs media
They separated the control plane (signaling) from the data plane (media). Signaling services handle meeting setup, roster, and control messages; media servers (SFUs) handle RTP/RTCP streams.

Benefits:
- Signaling can be horizontally scaled independently (small messages, many QoS-insensitive operations).
- Media servers can be optimized for CPU/network and autoscaled based on active streams.

Mermaid architecture (simplified):

```mermaid
graph LR
  ClientA --> EdgeSignaling[Edge Signaling (HTTP/WS)]
  ClientB --> EdgeSignaling
  EdgeSignaling --> Auth[Auth & Metadatastore]
  EdgeSignaling --> Dispatcher[Meeting Dispatcher]
  Dispatcher --> MediaPool[Media Edge Pool (SFU)]
  ClientA -->|RTP/UDP| MediaEdge1[Media Edge (SFU)]
  ClientB -->|RTP/UDP| MediaEdge1
  MediaEdge1 --> Recording[CDN / Recording Storage]
  MediaEdge1 --> TURN1[TURN Relay]
  MediaEdge1 --> CDN[Optional CDN for live large-broadcast]
```

### 2) Aggressive autoscaling of media servers using fine-grained metrics
Instead of simple CPU or pod-count autoscaling, Zoom used custom metrics: active peer count per server, total RTP sessions, and egress bandwidth. Autoscaling rules were tuned for:
- Scale-up: when active sessions per host > threshold OR bandwidth > 70%.
- Scale-down: when active sessions < threshold for a cooldown window.

This reduced over-provisioning and prevented slow reaction to bursts.

### 3) Protocol & network optimizations
- Prioritize UDP (RTP) with optimized jitter buffers and SVC (Scalable Video Coding) to reduce encoding/decoding cost and improve resilience to packet loss.
- Reduce TURN reliance by better ICE candidate harvesting: prefer local LAN/host candidates and keep-alive pinholes; only escalate to TURN when direct connectivity fails.
- Smart TURN selection: used regional TURNs and per-customer egress policies to reduce cross-region bandwidth.

### 4) Edge POP expansion and peering
They expanded edge Points-of-Presence (POPs) and improved peering with major last-mile ISPs. That reduced median network RTT and packet loss for many users.

### 5) Admission control & graceful degradation
When capacity flattened, Zoom implemented admission control: lower-fidelity join paths, prioritization for authenticated/paid customers, and soft-failures (join with audio-only if video capacity constrained).

### 6) Instrumentation, monitoring, and automated runbooks
- Instrumented per-region join latency, SFU CPU/bandwidth, TURN bandwidth, and packet loss.
- Automated incident playbooks for sudden region spikes.
- Health checks fed into the dispatcher so new joins avoided unhealthy POPs.

## Results (Before vs After)
| Metric | Before (peak surge) | After improvements |
|--------|---------------------:|--------------------:|
| Daily participants | ~300M (spike) | supported same scale reliably |
| Median join time (stressed regions) | 6–8s | 1.5–2s |
| Tail join time (95th) | >20s | ~6s |
| TURN bandwidth cost | Very high, exploding | Reduced by ~40% via candidate/peering optimizations |
| Manual capacity ops overhead | High (manual provisioning) | Reduced ~70% via autoscaling and automation |
| Outage incidents caused by scale | Multiple incidents during surge | Far fewer (SLA improvements; fewer user-impacting incidents) |

> Note: Zoom publicly reported jumps to ~300M daily meeting participants in April 2020; the numbers above reflect the engineering response rather than a single public metric.

## Visual: flow of a meeting join
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[User Client] --> S[Edge Signaling]
  S --> A[Auth Service]
  S --> D[Dispatcher]
  D --> M[Assign Media Edge]
  U -->|ICE (STUN/TURN)| M
  M --> REC[Recording Storage/CDN]
  M --> MON[Monitoring & Metrics]
```

## Why these decisions worked
- Separating signaling and media allowed different scaling profiles and shorter failure domains.
- Autoscaling on business metrics (active sessions + bandwidth) is far more effective for media services than CPU-only scaling.
- Reducing TURN usage and improving peering directly cut bandwidth costs and lowered latency.
- Admission control kept the system available by trading off fidelity when resources were constrained instead of failing entirely.

## Tradeoffs and lessons learned
- More POPs and peering reduce latency but increase operational complexity and cost — you must automate deployment and health checks.
- Aggressive autoscaling requires quick, accurate metrics and safeguards to avoid oscillation (use cooldown windows and hysteresis).
- Admission control policy decisions have product implications; choose defaults that protect paid customers while minimizing user confusion.

## Postmortem & culture: automation + chaos
Zoom doubled down on runbooks, automated regression testing for media stack, and introduced chaos-style failure drills for edge POPs and TURN saturation. That cultural investment decreased incident MTTR and helped the team respond to future spikes faster.

## Short checklist for teams facing similar surges
- Separate control and media planes.
- Use custom autoscaling metrics tied to active media sessions and bandwidth.
- Optimize ICE/TURN flow to avoid trivial TURN usage.
- Expand edge POPs and ISP peering where user pain is concentrated.
- Implement admission control before failures become hard outages.
keyTakeaways: Separate signaling and media so you can scale them independently — media needs autoscaling on active sessions and bandwidth, not just CPU.
Optimize NAT traversal: prefer local candidates and regionally distributed TURNs; reducing TURN usage can cut bandwidth costs by ~30–50%.
Automate ops: instrument per-region metrics, tie dispatcher logic to health signals, and use admission control to avoid total failures under overload.
companyCaseStudy.codeExample:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2beta2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: media-sfu-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: media-sfu
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 200
  metrics:
  - type: External
    external:
      metric:
        name: active_sessions_per_pod
      target:
        type: AverageValue
        averageValue: "200"  # scale when average active sessions per pod exceeds 200
  - type: External
    external:
      metric:
        name: egress_bandwidth_bytes
      target:
        type: AverageValue
        averageValue: "700000000"  # 700MB/s threshold

concept.title: Find It Fast: Practical Guide to Database Indexing & Query Optimization
concept.summary: Slow queries cost revenue and developer hours. Indexing and simple query optimizations let databases find the rows you need in milliseconds instead of scanning millions of rows — when used correctly. This guide explains the why, how, and common pitfalls with analogies, diagrams, before/after examples, and runnable SQL tips.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Imagine a library with no catalogue: every time you look for a book, the librarian scans every shelf. That’s a full table scan. Indexes are the library's card catalogue — they point directly to where a record lives. Good indexes can turn a multi-second query into a sub-10ms lookup. Bad or missing indexes create unpredictable latency, CPU waste, and cascading timeouts in services.

---

## Core idea (analogy)

- Table = library shelves
- Row = a book
- Index = card catalogue sorted by key
- Query with WHERE = asking the librarian for books by a property (author, title)

If you search by author and there is an author index, the librarian goes straight to the author card and fetches matching books quickly. If no index exists, they scan every shelf.

---

## How it works (flow)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Query] --> Planner[Query Planner / Optimizer]
  Planner -->|Has usable index?| CheckIndex{Index usable?}
  CheckIndex -->|Yes| IndexScan[Index Scan (seek by index)]
  CheckIndex -->|No| SeqScan[Sequential Scan]
  IndexScan --> Fetch[Fetch rows from table via pointer]
  SeqScan --> Fetch
  Fetch --> Result[Return result set]
```

---

## Common patterns: when to add an index

- Filtering: WHERE columns frequently used (highly selective)
- Joins: columns used in JOIN conditions
- Sorting: ORDER BY columns (can avoid sort if same index covers filter + order)
- Uniqueness: PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE constraints
- Covering index: index contains all columns needed for query (no table fetch)

When *not* to add an index: low-selectivity columns (boolean flags, tiny enums), tables with heavy write volume where index maintenance cost outweighs read benefit.

---

## Types of indexes (short)

- B-tree: general-purpose, ordered comparisons (>=, <, =). Default in most DBs.
- Hash: equality-only in some DBs (Postgres has hash but uncommon).
- GIN/GiST: inverted indexes for arrays, full-text, JSONB.
- BRIN: tiny index for very large, append-only/timestamp-ordered tables (Postgres).

---

## Examples & code

1) A simple filter:

Before: no index

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- planner picks a seq scan if no index exists
```

Create index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id);
-- or for faster lookups and covering:
CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id, created_at);
```

After: planner can use index

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- now you see Index Scan using orders_user_id_idx ...
```

2) Covering index to avoid fetching table rows:

```sql
-- Query needs only order_id and total
SELECT order_id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'paid';

-- Create covering index (include or composite depending on DB)
-- PostgreSQL: composite index with both columns (order_id likely part of PK, or use INCLUDE for non-key cols)
CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id, status, order_id);
-- PostgreSQL (better):
CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id, status) INCLUDE (order_id, total);
```

3) Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the plan and timing:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Look for: Index Scan vs Seq Scan, actual time, rows
```

---

## BEFORE / AFTER comparison

| Scenario | BEFORE (no index) | AFTER (index added) |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Query: user lookup | Seq Scan, 1200 ms | Index Scan, 5 ms |
| Query: text search | Seq Scan, 2000 ms | GIN index, 20 ms |
| ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 | Sort + Seq Scan, 900 ms | Index scan using created_at, 10 ms |

---

## Visual: Query sequence (fast path)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>DB: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
  DB->>Planner: Plan
  Planner->>Index: Seek key user_id=42
  Index-->>Planner: pointers -> rows
  Planner->>Storage: Fetch rows by pointers
  Storage-->>Client: Result set (fast)
```

---

## Practical tips and pitfalls

1. Cardinality (selectivity) matters
- Indexes help only if the predicate selects a *small* fraction of rows. An index on a column where 90% of rows have the same value is often useless.

2. Composite index ordering
- For a composite index (a,b,c) the prefix matters. Queries filtering on (a) or (a,b) can use it, but (b) alone generally cannot.

3. Functions and implicit transforms
- WHERE LOWER(name) = 'alice' prevents a plain index on name. Use functional indexes or normalize data:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON users (LOWER(name));
-- then query: WHERE LOWER(name) = 'alice'
```

4. Leading wildcards defeat indexes
- LIKE '%term' usually cannot use a B-tree index. Use full-text search or trigram/Gin indexes.

5. ORDER BY + LIMIT can be satisfied by index
- If your WHERE and ORDER BY match an index's left-to-right columns, the planner can avoid sorting.

6. Index maintenance cost
- Each index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Don't over-index write-heavy tables. Measure write latency impact.

7. Index bloat / fragmentation
- Periodically monitor and vacuum/rebuild indexes (Postgres: VACUUM, REINDEX) for long-lived tables.

8. Statistics and planner hints
- Keep stats up to date (ANALYZE) — the planner depends on accurate cardinality estimates.

9. Beware of OR and complex OR predicates
- OR can prevent index use; consider UNION of two queries each using an index or rewrite logic.

10. Use the right index type
- JSONB queries -> GIN
- Full text -> tsvector + GIN
- Time-series append -> BRIN

---

## How to diagnose slow queries (practical checklist)

1. EXPLAIN ANALYZE the slow SQL — read the actual timings.
2. Check if planner used an index. If not, why? (function, data type mismatch, low selectivity)
3. Try an index-only plan (covering index) to see if it helps.
4. Test impact on writes: run a benchmark of inserts/updates with the index in a staging environment.
5. Monitor slow_query_log (MySQL) or pg_stat_statements (Postgres).

---

## When to avoid indexing

- Small tables (table scan is cheap)
- Columns used only in analytics scans across entire dataset
- Columns with very low cardinality (e.g., boolean flags) unless combined in composite indexes

---

## Short checklist before adding an index

- Is the column used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY or GROUP BY frequently?
- Is the predicate selective? (Estimate rows returned)
- Would a composite index cover multiple filters/orderings?
- Will the index slow down writes unacceptably?
- Did you test with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and measure before/after?

---

## Final thought

Indexing is one of the highest leverage optimizations for databases, but it requires measurement and thought. Treat indexes like specialized tools: the right one in the right place makes your queries fly; the wrong one wastes disk and slows writes.
keyTakeaways: Indexes let the DB find rows without scanning the whole table — think catalog vs. shelf-by-shelf search.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify index usage; composite index order, selectivity, and functions matter.
Avoid over-indexing: each index speeds reads but costs writes and storage — measure before/after.
